A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Signature-Informed Transformer research. All 19 pages of v1 and 21 pages of v2, including their appendices, equations, tables and figures, support comparison.

before.justification: v1 reports original portfolio backtests on three S&P 100 asset universes, component ablations, and transaction-cost and allocation-temperature experiments.

after.justification: v2 retains those empirical results and adds DOW30 and CSI300 evaluations, another baseline, and analyses of attention, training objectives, diversification and drawdowns.

M1.justification: The signature/calendar/asset embeddings, temporal and asset attention, query-conditioned signature bias, positive gate, softmax allocation and CVaR training objective are unchanged. Newly specifying signature depth and presenting gate diagnostics does not establish a revised method.

E1.justification: v2 retains the S&P 100 universes and adds DOW30 portfolios of 10 and 20 assets and CSI300 portfolios of 50 and 100 assets (Section 3.1; Tables 6–7). This substantially broadens the represented equity populations, particularly beyond U.S. equities.

E2.justification: RFormer, identified with Moreno-Pino et al.'s Rough Transformer, is added to the comparisons against SIT in Tables 1 and 5 and participates in the new market evaluations. All previously evaluated traditional and forecasting comparators remain.

E3.justification: The original chronological splits, training budget and portfolio metrics remain. New evaluation designs compare MSE and decision-focused training across eight forecasting backbones, measure signature-strength/attention correlations, and evaluate HHI and entropy over temperatures from 0.5 to 2.0. These materially expand the experimental controls and diagnostics.

E4.justification: Sections 3.4–3.6 and Appendix H add attention-use diagnostics, a within-backbone training-objective comparison, diversification sensitivity, and gate-coloured drawdown analysis. The original component ablations and transaction-cost/temperature heatmap are retained.

E5.justification: Table 2 newly marks paired-test significance against SIT at p < 0.05 and p < 0.001; v1 reports the same ablation means without these tests. Benchmark mean-plus-standard-deviation reporting is retained. Neither version specifies run counts or seeds, and v2 does not identify the paired test or pairing unit.

E6.justification: All original benchmark values, ablation means and transaction-cost heatmap values are retained. v2 adds RFormer and new-market results, attention-correlation means of 0.540 and 0.611, and objective/diversification/gate findings. The new results include exceptions to blanket superiority: DOW30-10 GMV has Sharpe 1.0394 versus SIT's 1.0312 (Table 6).

T1.justification: Section 3.4 introduces mathematical definitions of the signature-strength and inbound-attention scores used in its diagnostic. The existing lead–lag, attention-derivative and CVaR-dominance results and proofs are unchanged. Relabelling Theorem 3.1 as Proposition 2.1 does not itself change the mathematics.

C1.justification: The abstract broadens the empirical superiority claim from daily S&P 100 data to diverse equity universes. The three principal contributions—signature representations, signature-augmented attention and decision alignment—and the central conclusion remain.

C2.justification: v2 substantially expands interpretations of how signatures influence attention and risk-relevant information routing, how gate behaviour relates to volatile episodes, and how dimensionality affects objective mismatch. It also introduces a practical interpretation of temperature as diversification control. These extend the mechanism and applicability discussion beyond v1's ablation-based explanations.

D1.justification: New Appendix F specifies the previously underspecified forecasting-baseline pipeline: MSE training, frozen forecasts, historical-scenario CVaR optimization and a target-return constraint. Table 4 adds RFormer search settings and discloses SIT's signature depth of two. The code-access pointer changes from GitHub to an anonymous repository. These are documentation changes, not evidence that existing experiments were rerun.

R1.justification: v2 adds discussion and citation of Rough Transformer, replaces the Zhang–Zohren review citation with Hwang et al. (2025b), and explicitly attributes the lead–lag proposition to existing signature literature. Most related-work content and SIT's positioning remain unchanged after relocation to Appendix A.

P1.justification: The abstract is rewritten, related work moves from main Section 2 to Appendix A, and the LLM-use appendix is removed. Headings and cross-references are adjusted. Most existing introduction, methodology, proof and experimental prose is retained; much of the additional prose accompanies new scientific analyses.

P2.justification: The main paper changes from predominantly single-column to two-column formatting. v2 adds four diagnostic figures and two benchmark tables, expands comparison and hyperparameter tables, and annotates ablation significance. The original transaction-cost heatmap is retained as Figure 5 rather than Figure 3.

improvement.justification: Broader market validation, the relevant RFormer comparator, and within-backbone objective comparisons strengthen v1's empirical support, while Appendix F clarifies an important baseline implementation. These gains are tempered by new overinterpretations: Figure 4 does not support uniformly superior DFL performance, paired tests remain underspecified, and the time-varying gate analysis is not reconciled with the scalar-gate formulation. The net quality improvement is positive but limited.
